newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq clarifies its weapons declarations to U.N.
newsitem.headline: Iraq clarifies its weapons declarations to U.N.

text.p: Iraq has given the United Nations letters aimed at clarifying disclosures over its weapons of mass destruction after a senior U.N. arms inspector criticised Baghdad's original declarations as flawed and incomplete.

Deputy Chairman of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) Charles Duelfer said on Thursday the letters covered Iraq's disclosures on chemical, biological and missile programmes, which UNSCOM is charged with dismantling under terms of the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire.

"They are letters...to explain part of the Iraqi declarations," Duelfer told reporters as he left his hotel at the end of a four-day visit to Baghdad. "But they are not documents which could provide verification."

Duelfer said on Tuesday that "final" reports submitted by Iraq in August about its chemical, biological and missile systems appeared at first reading to have problems of error and omission in all three areas.
His comments sparked a robust response from Iraq's oil minister and former head of its Military Industrialistion Commission Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed.

Rasheed said Iraq had supplied "detailed, complete and comprehensive" reports to UNSCOM and suggested Duelfer, an American, was following a U.S. policy to slow down UNSCOM's work and block the final lifting of six-year sanctions on Iraq.
Approval of the reports, known as Full, Final and Complete Disclosures (FFCDs), is a key requirement for ending the sanctions imposed on Iraq over its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Duelfer described his second meeting with Rashid on Wednesday as frank and lively. "His criticism of my presentation I do not accept," he added.

"The Commission has a far better understanding now of the past activities of Iraq with respect to weapons of mass destruction...(but) serious problems remain," Duelfer said. "The problems include gaps in their declarations."
He said UNSCOM would not be rushed into giving Iraq a clean bill of health.

"I would remind you that a year ago we were subject to the same criticism when the Iraqi government claimed it had given everything to the Commission," Duelfer said. "Shortly after that Iraq finally acknowledged that it had a very large offensive biological weapons programme."
The latest row over Iraq's disclosures follows a series of stand offs in June and July when UNSCOM officials were denied access to inspection sites.
Iraq said its security was being jeopardised by UNSCOM requests to inspect installations linked to presidential security or Iraq's elite Republican Guards.
Duelfer said he hoped inspection teams would have the "unrestricted and unconstrained access that has been promised."
His talks with Rasheed were intended to be candid and straightforward, he said.

"Unfortunately they were attacking me because of my nationality. I am not a cruise missile," Duelfer said. "We are working very hard at our task (and) the pace of our progress is dependent on cooperation from Iraq, not attacks from Iraq."
